topics.name: Antibodies
topics.kicker: Y-shaped immune proteins · Made by B cells to grab specific antigens
topics.dates: First found in blood serum in 1890
topics.briefing: Antibodies are Y-shaped proteins that your B cells make to fight invaders. Each kind fits just one target, called an antigen, the way a key fits one lock, and your body can make billions of different kinds. When antibodies latch onto a virus or a toxin, they can block it or tag it for destruction, and vaccines work by teaching your body to make the right ones before you ever get sick.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Rodney Porter used the enzyme papain to cut these molecules into three pieces: two identical arms that grab targets and one stem. Porter shared the 1972 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Gerald Edelman, who showed that these molecules are built from separate heavy and light protein chains.
tossups.r: Plasma cells, which develop from B cells, release them into the blood. For 10 points, name these Y-shaped proteins that bind to antigens.

tossups.p: Susumu Tonegawa [“toh-neh-GAH-wah”] won the 1987 Nobel Prize for showing that young B cells cut and rejoin gene segments to build a huge variety of these molecules. That shuffling, called V(D)J recombination, lets the body make billions of different kinds of them.
tossups.r: Each kind fits one antigen like a key in a lock. For 10 points, name these Y-shaped proteins made by B cells.

tossups.p: In 1975, Georges Köhler and César Milstein fused B cells with cancer cells to create hybridomas, cell lines that pump out endless identical copies of one of these molecules. Medicines built from such identical copies have names ending in “-mab.” Köhler and Milstein shared the 1984 Nobel Prize with Niels Jerne.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these Y-shaped proteins of the immune system, which B cells make to bind antigens.

tossups.p: In 1890, Emil von Behring and Kitasato Shibasaburō showed that blood serum from animals given small doses of tetanus or diphtheria toxin could protect other animals, because the serum held these molecules. Behring won the first Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, in 1901, for that “serum therapy.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these proteins, made by B cells, that neutralize toxins by binding to antigens.

tossups.p: Paul Ehrlich’s “side-chain theory” proposed that cells grow extra receptors that break off into the blood and become these molecules. Ehrlich shared the 1908 Nobel Prize with Élie Metchnikoff [“MECH-nih-koff”], who discovered that some white blood cells swallow germs.
tossups.r: Those cells eat germs more easily after these molecules coat them, a process called opsonization [“op-suh-nuh-ZAY-shun”]. For 10 points, name these Y-shaped proteins made by B cells.

tossups.p: People with type O blood carry two kinds of these molecules in their plasma, one that binds the A marker and one that binds the B marker on red blood cells. People with type AB blood carry neither kind, which is why they can receive red cells of any ABO type.
tossups.r: When these molecules meet mismatched cells, the cells clump together. For 10 points, name these Y-shaped proteins of the immune system.

tossups.p: One class of these molecules is the only class that crosses the placenta, protecting a baby during its first months of life. Another class guards wet surfaces such as tears, saliva, and mucus, and it is also passed to babies in breast milk.
tossups.r: Those classes are IgG and IgA. For 10 points, name these Y-shaped proteins, which are made by B cells.

tossups.p: The M class of these molecules links five units into a star-shaped cluster held together by a small J chain, and it is the first class made during a new infection. The A class often travels in pairs.
tossups.r: Memory B cells help the body make them faster the second time. For 10 points, name these Y-shaped proteins that bind to antigens.

tossups.p: The E class of these molecules coats mast cells, which release histamine when an allergen such as pollen latches onto that coating, causing sneezing and itching. That class also helps the body fight parasitic worms.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these Y-shaped proteins, made by plasma cells, that each recognize one specific antigen.

tossups.p: The branch of the immune system that depends on these molecules is called humoral immunity, from an old word for the body’s fluids. When these molecules coat a bacterium, they can switch on the complement system, a group of blood proteins that can punch holes in the germ’s membrane.
tossups.r: Human versions have two heavy and two light chains in a Y shape. For 10 points, name these immune proteins that bind antigens.

tossups.p: In myasthenia gravis [“my-us-THEE-nee-uh GRAV-iss”], these molecules block the receptors that let muscles respond to the nerve signal acetylcholine, causing weakness. In Graves’ disease, these molecules switch on the thyroid gland and make it overactive.
tossups.r: Normally, B cells make them to fight germs. For 10 points, name these Y-shaped proteins that bind to antigens.

tossups.p: To make antivenom, scientists often inject horses or sheep with small doses of snake venom and later collect these molecules from the animals’ blood. Giving a patient these molecules ready-made is called passive immunity, because the patient’s own body did not make them.
tossups.r: Vaccines, by contrast, train the body to make its own. For 10 points, name these proteins that plasma cells release to bind antigens.

tossups.p: The tips of both arms of these molecules hold variable regions that fit one epitope, the small part of an antigen they recognize. A flexible hinge joins those arms to a stem called the Fc region, which other immune cells can grab.
tossups.r: They latch onto germs and toxins so the body can destroy them. For 10 points, name these Y-shaped proteins made by B cells and plasma cells.

tossups.p: The ELISA [“ee-LY-zuh”] lab test links these molecules to an enzyme that causes a color change when they find their target. Home rapid tests for COVID-19 also use these molecules, which grab virus proteins and make a colored line appear.
tossups.r: In the body, B cells make them. For 10 points, name these Y-shaped proteins that recognize antigens.

tossups.p: Frank Macfarlane Burnet’s clonal selection theory explained that each B cell makes just one kind of these molecules, and only the B cells whose kind matches an invader multiply. Some of those B cells become long-lived memory cells.
tossups.r: Vaccines work by training the body to make these molecules. For 10 points, name these Y-shaped proteins that bind antigens.

clues.t: Y-shaped proteins that the immune system makes to latch onto antigens, the markers on germs and other invaders
Made by B cells; activated B cells called plasma cells release huge numbers of them
Each kind fits one specific antigen, the way a key fits one lock
Vaccines train the body to make them, and memory B cells make them faster the next time
They block viruses and toxins and tag germs so other immune cells can destroy them
Built from two heavy chains and two light chains, held together by disulfide bonds
The tips of the Y’s arms hold variable regions that fit the antigen; the stem is the Fc region
The small part of an antigen that one of them recognizes is an epitope; a flexible hinge lets the arms swing
Five classes: IgG (the most common in blood), IgA, IgM, IgE, and IgD
IgG is the only class that crosses the placenta; IgA guards tears, saliva, and mucus and is passed on in breast milk
IgE makes mast cells release histamine in allergies, and it helps fight parasitic worms
IgM, the first class made in a new infection, joins five units into a star-shaped pentamer with a J chain
Type O plasma carries anti-A and anti-B kinds, and type AB plasma carries neither; mismatched blood clumps (agglutination)
Receiving ready-made ones, from a mother or an antivenom shot, is passive immunity; making your own is active immunity
Coating a germ so that phagocytes can eat it more easily is called opsonization
Rodney Porter and Gerald Edelman shared the 1972 Nobel Prize for their structure; Porter cut them apart with the enzyme papain
Susumu Tonegawa won the 1987 Nobel Prize for showing how shuffled gene segments (V(D)J recombination) create their huge variety
Georges Köhler and César Milstein made the first hybridomas in 1975 to mass-produce monoclonal ones; they shared the 1984 Nobel Prize with Niels Jerne
Medicines made from monoclonal ones have names ending in “-mab”
Emil von Behring and Kitasato Shibasaburō found them in serum (1890); Behring won the first Nobel in Physiology or Medicine (1901) for serum therapy
Paul Ehrlich’s “side-chain theory” tried to explain how cells make them; he shared the 1908 Nobel Prize with Élie Metchnikoff
Frank Macfarlane Burnet’s clonal selection theory: each B cell makes one kind, and the B cells that match an invader multiply
Their branch of defense is called humoral immunity, from an old word for body fluids; they can also switch on complement proteins that punch holes in germs
In myasthenia gravis they block muscle receptors for acetylcholine; in Graves’ disease they overstimulate the thyroid gland
ELISA tests and home rapid tests use them, linked to enzymes or dyes, to detect specific proteins
Antivenom is often made by giving horses or sheep small doses of venom and collecting these proteins from their blood

trap.title: Antibody or antigen?
trap.body: The two words sound alike and show up in the same sentences. An antigen is the marker on a germ, a pollen grain, or a red blood cell that gets recognized; an antibody is the Y-shaped protein the body makes to grab it. Players also blurt “B cells,” the cells that make antibodies, or “antibiotics,” the germ-killing medicines.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “these proteins” or “these Y-shaped molecules,” or mentions heavy and light chains, say antibodies (or immunoglobulins). Say antigen only for “this substance” that the immune system recognizes, and B cells only for “these cells” that make them.
trap.line: Real answer line: Antibodies (accept antibody or immunoglobulins; do not accept “antigens” or “antibiotics”)

topics.name: Gymnosperms
topics.kicker: “Naked seed” plants · Conifers, cycads, ginkgos, and gnetophytes
topics.dates: First appeared more than 300 million years ago
topics.briefing: Gymnosperms are seed plants whose seeds sit out in the open, usually on the scales of a cone, instead of being wrapped inside a fruit; their name means “naked seed” in Greek. The group includes pines, spruces, and other conifers, plus palm-like cycads, the fan-leaved ginkgo, and unusual gnetophytes such as the two-leaved desert plant _Welwitschia_. They ruled forests in the age of the dinosaurs, and the tallest known living tree and the biggest known single tree are both conifers.
topics.answerHtml: Gymnosperms (accept gymnosperm or Gymnospermae; prompt on seed plants; do not accept “conifers” or “angiosperms”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: _Welwitschia_ [“wel-WITCH-ee-uh”], a desert plant that grows only two leaves in its whole life, belongs to a small division of this group called the gnetophytes [“NEE-toh-fyts”]. Unlike the rest of this group, gnetophytes have water-carrying vessels in their xylem, like flowering plants.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of seed plants, including pines and other conifers, whose seeds are not enclosed in fruit.

tossups.p: Unlike flowering plants, these plants never form a triploid endosperm; instead, the food stored in their seeds is haploid tissue from the female gametophyte. Many of them catch pollen on a sticky “pollination drop” that oozes from the tiny opening of each ovule.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of seed plants, which includes cycads and conifers, whose name means “naked seed.”

tossups.p: _Ginkgo biloba_ [“GINK-oh by-LOH-buh”], the only living species in its division of this group, has fan-shaped leaves, and its female trees make seeds with a fleshy coat that smells like rancid butter. Ginkgos and cycads in this group still make swimming sperm.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of seed plants, which also includes conifers, whose seeds are not enclosed in a fruit.

tossups.p: The sago palm is not a true palm but a cycad, a member of this group. Cycads grow special coral-shaped roots that house nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria, and they were common in the age of the dinosaurs.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of seed plants, including pines and spruces, that often carry their seeds on cones.

tossups.p: In pines, members of this group, fertilization happens more than a year after a pollen grain lands on a seed cone, and the seeds can take about two years to mature. Pine pollen grains have two air sacs that help them ride the wind.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of plants, which includes conifers, cycads, and the ginkgo, that do not enclose their seeds in fruit.

tossups.p: Lodgepole pines and jack pines in this group make serotinous [“seh-ROT-ih-nus”] cones, which stay sealed with resin until the heat of a forest fire opens them. Amber is fossilized resin, and much of it came from trees in this group.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of “naked seed” plants that includes pines, firs, and spruces.

tossups.p: A coast redwood named Hyperion, the tallest known living tree, belongs to this group, as does a Great Basin bristlecone pine called Methuselah, one of the oldest known living trees. So does General Sherman, a giant sequoia in California that is the biggest known living single tree by volume.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of seed plants, including conifers, whose seeds are not enclosed in an ovary.

tossups.p: The cancer drug paclitaxel [“pak-lih-TAK-sul”], sold as Taxol, was first found in the bark of the Pacific yew, a tree in this group. Unlike pines, yews do not make woody seed cones; instead, each seed sits in a fleshy red cup called an aril.
tossups.r: Most members of this group are evergreen. For 10 points, name this group of seed plants that also includes pines and other conifers.

tossups.p: The dawn redwood was known only from fossils until living trees were found in China in the 1940s, and the Wollemi [“WALL-uh-my”] pine was discovered in an Australian canyon in 1994. Both are “living fossils” from this ancient group of plants.
tossups.r: This group dominated forests during the age of the dinosaurs. For 10 points, name this group of plants with “naked” seeds, including conifers.

tossups.p: The leaves of many members of this group are narrow needles with a thick waxy cuticle and stomata sunk into pits, adaptations that help them keep water through winters when the soil is frozen.
tossups.r: Members of this group dominate the taiga across Canada and Russia. For 10 points, name this group of seed plants, which includes pines, spruces, and firs.

tossups.p: The wood of most members of this group, called softwood, is made almost entirely of water-carrying tracheids [“TRAY-kee-idz”] rather than the wide vessels of hardwoods. Conifer phloem uses sieve cells helped by Strasburger [“SHTRAHS-boor-ger”] cells instead of companion cells.
tossups.r: Pine resin from this group can be made into turpentine. For 10 points, name this group of plants whose seeds develop on the scales of cones.

tossups.p: Each scale of a pine’s seed cone carries two ovules, and pollen enters each ovule through a tiny opening called the micropyle [“MY-kroh-pyle”]. When the cone dries and opens, its seeds, many with a papery wing, flutter away on the wind.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of seed plants, including conifers, whose seeds are not enclosed in fruit.

tossups.p: Larches, bald cypresses, and dawn redwoods are unusual members of this group because they are deciduous, dropping all their needles every fall. Bald cypresses growing in swamps send up woody bumps called “knees” around their trunks.
tossups.r: Most other members of this group, such as pines, stay green all year. For 10 points, name this group of plants whose seeds are not enclosed in fruit.

tossups.p: Ginkgophyta [“gink-GOFF-ih-tuh”], which has just one living species, is one of this group’s four living divisions, along with the cycads and the gnetophytes. This group appeared more than 300 million years ago, long before flowering plants, and dominated the world’s forests during the Mesozoic Era.
tossups.r: The fourth division is the conifers. For 10 points, name this group of seed plants whose name means “naked seed.”

tossups.p: _Gnetum_, a tropical member of this group, has broad leaves that look like those of flowering plants. In the same group, the “berries” of junipers are really tiny cones whose scales have turned fleshy and fused together, and the edible “nuts” of piñon [“PIN-yohn”] pines are actually seeds.
tossups.r: This group also includes the spruces and firs often used as Christmas trees. For 10 points, name this group of seed plants that carry seeds on cones rather than in fruit.

clues.t: Seed plants whose seeds are not enclosed in a fruit; the name means “naked seed” in Greek
Many carry their seeds on the scales of cones
Include conifers such as pines, spruces, firs (popular Christmas trees), cedars, and redwoods
Their flowering relatives, the angiosperms, enclose seeds inside an ovary that becomes a fruit
Most are evergreen, keeping needle- or scale-shaped leaves all year
Four living groups: conifers, cycads, the ginkgo, and gnetophytes
Most are pollinated by wind; pine pollen grains have two air sacs that help them float
Conifer wood, called softwood, is made mostly of tracheids, not wide vessels; pine resin is distilled into turpentine
Conifers dominate the taiga, or boreal forest, across Canada, Scandinavia, and Russia
Needles with a thick waxy cuticle and sunken stomata help them keep water through frozen winters
_Ginkgo biloba_, a “living fossil” with fan-shaped leaves, is the only living species in its division; female trees make smelly seeds
Appeared more than 300 million years ago and dominated forests in the age of the dinosaurs, the Mesozoic Era
Gnetophytes (_Gnetum_, _Ephedra_, and _Welwitschia_) are the only ones with xylem vessels; _Gnetum_ has broad leaves like a flowering plant’s
_Welwitschia_ of the Namib Desert grows only two leaves in its whole life
No triploid endosperm: the food in their seeds is haploid tissue from the female gametophyte
Many catch pollen on a sticky pollination drop at the micropyle, the opening of each ovule; each pine cone scale holds two ovules
Cycads and the ginkgo still make swimming sperm
Cycads such as the sago palm look like palms; their coral-shaped (coralloid) roots house nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria
In pines, fertilization comes more than a year after pollination, and seeds take about two years to mature
Lodgepole and jack pines make serotinous cones that stay sealed with resin until a fire opens them; fossilized resin is amber
Record trees: Hyperion, a coast redwood (tallest known); General Sherman, a giant sequoia (biggest living single tree by volume); Methuselah, a bristlecone pine (among the oldest)
The Pacific yew, whose seeds sit in red fleshy arils instead of cones, gave the cancer drug Taxol (paclitaxel)
The dawn redwood (found alive in China in the 1940s) and the Wollemi pine (found in Australia in 1994) are “living fossils”
Larches, bald cypresses, and dawn redwoods are deciduous, dropping their needles every fall; bald cypresses grow woody “knees”
Conifer phloem uses sieve cells helped by Strasburger cells instead of companion cells
Juniper “berries” are really fleshy cones, and the “nuts” of piñon pines are really seeds

trap.title: Not just conifers
trap.body: Most tossups on this group mention pines, spruces, and cones, so players blurt “conifers.” But conifers are only one of four living divisions: cycads, the ginkgo, and gnetophytes like _Welwitschia_ belong to this group too, so the narrower answer is wrong when the question asks for the whole group. The opposite trap is “angiosperms,” the flowering plants that enclose their seeds in fruit.
trap.fix: “This group of seed plants,” “naked seeds,” or a mix of cycads, ginkgos, and pines means gymnosperms. Say conifers only for “these cone-bearing trees” when every clue stays on pines and their relatives. Fruit, flowers, or double fertilization mean angiosperms.
trap.line: Real answer line: Gymnosperms (accept gymnosperm or Gymnospermae; prompt on seed plants; do not accept “conifers” or “angiosperms”)

topics.name: Adrenal glands
topics.kicker: Paired glands on top of the kidneys · Make cortisol and adrenaline
topics.briefing: Your two adrenal glands sit on top of your kidneys like little caps, and each one is really two glands in one. The outer cortex makes steroid hormones such as cortisol, which helps you handle stress, and aldosterone, which balances salt and water. The inner medulla, wired to your nervous system, floods your blood with adrenaline when something startles you.
topics.answerHtml: Adrenal glands (accept adrenals or suprarenal glands; prompt on adrenal cortex or adrenal medulla; do not accept “kidneys” or “adrenaline”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The outer layer of these glands has three zones: the zona glomerulosa [“gloh-mair-yoo-LOH-suh”] makes aldosterone, the zona fasciculata [“fuh-sik-yoo-LAH-tuh”] makes cortisol, and the zona reticularis [“reh-tik-yoo-LAIR-iss”] makes androgens such as DHEA. Their order, from the outside in, can be remembered with the letters “GFR.”
tossups.r: The inner part of these glands makes adrenaline. For 10 points, name these glands that sit on top of the kidneys.

tossups.p: Edward Kendall, Philip Hench, and Tadeus Reichstein [“RYKE-shtine”] shared the 1950 Nobel Prize for studying hormones from the outer layer of these glands. Hench used one of those hormones, cortisone, to treat people with rheumatoid arthritis.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these glands, perched on top of the kidneys, that make cortisol and adrenaline.

tossups.p: In 1855, Thomas Addison described a disease in which these glands make too little cortisol and aldosterone, often causing tiredness, weakness, and darkened skin. President John F. Kennedy had that disease.
tossups.r: Their inner medulla makes epinephrine. For 10 points, name these glands, located on top of the kidneys, that make the stress hormone cortisol.

tossups.p: In 1856, Charles-Édouard Brown-Séquard [“brown-say-KAR”] showed that animals could not survive after both of these glands were removed. About three centuries earlier, Bartolomeo Eustachi [“ay-oo-STAH-kee”], the namesake of the tube linking the middle ear to the throat, had first described them.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these small glands that sit on top of the kidneys and release epinephrine.

tossups.p: When blood pressure drops, the hormone angiotensin II [“an-jee-oh-TEN-sin two”] tells the outer layer of these glands to release aldosterone, which makes the body keep more sodium and water. A tumor in one of these glands that makes too much aldosterone causes Conn’s syndrome.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these glands perched on top of the kidneys, whose inner part makes adrenaline.

tossups.p: The hypothalamus releases CRH, which tells the pituitary gland to send out ACTH, which in turn tells these glands to release cortisol. Doctors call that chain of command the HPA axis.
tossups.r: The inner medulla of these glands releases epinephrine during stress. For 10 points, name these glands found on top of the kidneys.

tossups.p: Harvey Cushing, a pioneering brain surgeon, described a condition in which the body has too much of a hormone made by these glands. That hormone normally rises each morning and helps the body handle stress by raising blood sugar.
tossups.r: That hormone is cortisol. For 10 points, name these glands that sit on top of the kidneys.

tossups.p: The inner part of each of these glands is packed with chromaffin [“KROH-muh-fin”] cells, which develop from the same neural crest tissue as many nerve cells. Nerve fibers of the sympathetic nervous system signal those cells with acetylcholine.
tossups.r: Those cells then release epinephrine. For 10 points, name these glands located on top of the kidneys.

tossups.p: The right one of these glands is shaped like a pyramid, while the left one is shaped more like a crescent. Each is wrapped in fat, and their name comes from Latin words meaning “near the kidneys.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these glands, which sit on the kidneys, whose medulla makes adrenaline and whose cortex makes cortisol.

tossups.p: A rare tumor called pheochromocytoma [“fee-oh-kroh-moh-sye-TOH-muh”] grows in the inner part of one of these glands and releases bursts of extra epinephrine and norepinephrine, causing headaches, sweating, and a pounding heartbeat.
tossups.r: Normally, these glands release large amounts of those hormones only in “fight-or-flight” moments. For 10 points, name these glands on top of the kidneys.

tossups.p: Cells in the outer layer of these glands store droplets of cholesterol, which enzymes in their mitochondria convert into pregnenolone [“preg-NEE-nuh-lohn”], the first step in making steroid hormones. Those fatty droplets give the outer layer its yellow color.
tossups.r: Those hormones include cortisol and aldosterone. For 10 points, name these glands located on top of the kidneys.

tossups.p: Hans Selye [“SEL-yay”] found that rats under constant stress developed enlarged versions of these glands, along with shrunken thymus glands and stomach ulcers. That discovery led him to describe the “general adaptation syndrome.”
tossups.r: These glands release cortisol and adrenaline during stress. For 10 points, name these glands that sit on top of the kidneys.

tossups.p: Hydrocortisone creams and drugs such as prednisone copy a hormone from the outer layer of these glands, which calms swelling and slows the immune system. That hormone also helps the liver make new glucose between meals.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these glands, found atop the kidneys, that make cortisol and adrenaline.

tossups.p: Two groups of steroid hormones made by these glands are the mineralocorticoids, which control salt balance, and the glucocorticoids, which help control blood sugar. The main hormone of the first group is aldosterone.
tossups.r: The inner medulla of these glands makes epinephrine. For 10 points, name these glands located on top of each kidney.

tossups.p: In 1901, Japanese chemist Jokichi Takamine [“tah-kah-MEE-nay”] isolated a hormone from these glands of animals, a few years after John Jacob Abel had studied extracts of them. Takamine later helped arrange Japan’s 1912 gift of cherry trees to Washington, D.C.
tossups.r: The hormone he isolated is better known as adrenaline. For 10 points, name these glands that sit on top of the kidneys.

clues.t: A pair of small glands, one sitting on top of each kidney
Release epinephrine (adrenaline), the “fight-or-flight” hormone
Release cortisol, the body’s main stress hormone
Each has an outer cortex and an inner medulla
The medulla releases epinephrine and norepinephrine when nerves of the sympathetic nervous system signal it
The cortex makes steroid hormones, such as cortisol and aldosterone, from cholesterol
Aldosterone makes the kidneys keep sodium and water and get rid of potassium
ACTH from the pituitary gland tells the cortex to release cortisol
Cortisol raises blood sugar, calms inflammation, and slows the immune system; its level peaks in the morning
Addison’s disease (described by Thomas Addison in 1855): too little cortisol and aldosterone; John F. Kennedy had it
Cushing’s syndrome, named for brain surgeon Harvey Cushing: the body has too much cortisol
Cortex hormones include mineralocorticoids (salt balance, like aldosterone) and glucocorticoids (blood sugar, like cortisol)
Their name comes from Latin words meaning “near the kidneys”
The cortex has three zones, outside in: glomerulosa (aldosterone), fasciculata (cortisol), and reticularis (androgens such as DHEA), or “GFR”
Edward Kendall, Philip Hench, and Tadeus Reichstein shared the 1950 Nobel Prize for cortex hormones; Hench treated rheumatoid arthritis with cortisone
Charles-Édouard Brown-Séquard showed in 1856 that animals cannot survive without them
Bartolomeo Eustachi, namesake of the ear’s Eustachian tube, first described them in the 1500s
The medulla’s chromaffin cells come from the neural crest, like nerve cells, and respond to the nerve signal acetylcholine
The HPA axis: CRH from the hypothalamus tells the pituitary to send ACTH, which tells these glands to release cortisol
Angiotensin II triggers aldosterone release when blood pressure drops; a tumor making too much aldosterone causes Conn’s syndrome
Pheochromocytoma, a rare tumor of the medulla, releases bursts of epinephrine and norepinephrine
The right one is shaped like a pyramid and the left one like a crescent
Cortex cells store cholesterol droplets, which make the cortex yellow, and turn cholesterol into pregnenolone in their mitochondria
Hans Selye found enlarged ones in stressed rats, along with shrunken thymus glands and ulcers, and described the “general adaptation syndrome”
Hydrocortisone creams and drugs like prednisone copy their cortisol to calm swelling
Jokichi Takamine isolated epinephrine from them in 1901, after work by John Jacob Abel; he later helped arrange Japan’s 1912 cherry-tree gift

trap.title: Gland, not hormone
trap.body: Tossups on these glands are packed with their hormones (epinephrine, norepinephrine, cortisol, and aldosterone), and players buzz with a hormone instead of the gland. Others answer “kidneys,” the organs underneath them, or name just one layer, the cortex or the medulla.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “these glands” or “these organs,” say adrenal glands. Name a hormone only for “this hormone” or “this compound.” The kidneys filter blood and make urine; the glands on top of them make hormones.
trap.line: Real answer line: Adrenal glands (accept adrenals or suprarenal glands; prompt on adrenal cortex or adrenal medulla; do not accept “kidneys” or “adrenaline”)

topics.name: Blood clotting
topics.kicker: How blood seals a wound · Platelets plus a cascade that builds fibrin
topics.dates: Starts within moments of an injury
topics.briefing: Blood clotting, also called coagulation, is how your body plugs a leak. When you cut yourself, tiny cell pieces called platelets pile up at the wound, then a chain reaction of proteins turns a dissolved protein called fibrinogen into sticky threads of fibrin that trap blood cells in a gel-like mesh. The process needs calcium and vitamin K, and people with the inherited disorder hemophilia have trouble completing it.
topics.answerHtml: Blood clotting (accept coagulation; prompt on hemostasis or blood clots; do not accept “agglutination”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Henrik Dam named a vitamin with the letter K after the Danish and German spelling of this process, because chicks fed a diet lacking that vitamin bled easily. Dam shared the 1943 Nobel Prize with Edward Doisy for work on that vitamin.
tossups.r: Platelets and threads of fibrin help this process seal wounds. For 10 points, name this process in which blood thickens into a gel to stop bleeding.

tossups.p: The factors that drive this process are numbered with Roman numerals from I to XIII, though none is still called factor VI, and factor IV is simply calcium. Factor XIII finishes the job by cross-linking threads of fibrin into a sturdy mesh.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, which uses platelets and fibrin to seal a cut so it stops bleeding.

tossups.p: A 2009 DNA study of Russia’s last royal family showed that Queen Victoria’s descendants carried a gene variant for “Christmas disease,” a disorder of this process. That nickname honors Stephen Christmas, the first patient described with it, in 1952.
tossups.r: That disorder is a form of hemophilia. For 10 points, name this process in which platelets and fibrin seal a wound.

tossups.p: In 1926, Finnish doctor Erik von Willebrand studied families on the Åland [“OH-land”] Islands and described the most common inherited disorder of this process. The protein named for him helps platelets stick to collagen in a damaged blood vessel wall.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process in which blood thickens into a gel-like plug to seal a wound.

tossups.p: In the 1920s, cattle that ate spoiled sweet clover suffered deadly bleeding, a mystery that Karl Paul Link’s lab later solved by finding dicoumarol [“dy-KOO-muh-rawl”], a compound that blocks this process. Link’s team then developed warfarin, named for the Wisconsin Alumni Research Foundation.
tossups.r: Warfarin interferes with vitamin K, which the liver needs to make several proteins for this process. For 10 points, name this process that seals wounds with fibrin.

tossups.p: In 1916, medical student Jay McLean found a substance in dog liver that slows this process; it was later named heparin, from the Greek word for “liver.” Heparin works by boosting antithrombin, a protein that switches off key enzymes of this process.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process in which platelets and fibrin plug a leaking blood vessel.

tossups.p: Thrombin speeds up its own production during this process, a classic example of positive feedback. This process also needs calcium ions, so blood-collection tubes often contain citrate, which grabs calcium and keeps the sample liquid.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process in which blood forms a gel-like plug to stop bleeding.

tossups.p: The enzyme plasmin undoes the work of this process by chopping up fibrin, leaving fragments called D-dimers that doctors can measure. A drug called tPA turns plasminogen into plasmin and can dissolve blockages that cause some strokes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, which uses platelets and fibrin to seal damaged blood vessels.

tossups.p: Tissue factor, exposed when a blood vessel is damaged, starts the extrinsic pathway of this process, while the intrinsic pathway begins with factors already in the blood. Both pathways meet at factor X, which helps turn prothrombin into thrombin.
tossups.r: Thrombin then converts fibrinogen into fibrin. For 10 points, name this process that seals cuts and stops bleeding.

tossups.p: Vampire bat saliva contains draculin, a protein that blocks this process so blood keeps flowing while the bat feeds. Leeches use a different blocker of this process, called hirudin [“hih-ROO-din”], and mosquitoes and ticks also inject chemicals that block it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, involving platelets and fibrin, that stops bleeding at a wound.

tossups.p: An extract of horseshoe crab blood cells turns into a gel when it meets bacterial toxins, a version of this process that drug companies use to test medicines for contamination. In humans, this process turns the dissolved protein fibrinogen into solid threads.
tossups.r: Those threads are made of fibrin. For 10 points, name this process that stops bleeding from a wound.

tossups.p: Aspirin slows one part of this process by stopping platelets from making thromboxane A2, a chemical signal that calls more platelets to a wound. Platelets first stick to collagen exposed in a torn blood vessel.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that seals a wound with platelets and threads of fibrin.

tossups.p: Serum is the yellowish liquid left over after this process, because this process uses up fibrinogen; plasma, by contrast, still contains fibrinogen. The liver makes most of the proteins this process needs, including prothrombin and fibrinogen.
tossups.r: A scab is the dried result of this process on skin. For 10 points, name this process in which blood thickens into a gel to stop bleeding.

tossups.p: Newborn babies in many countries get a shot of vitamin K, because they are born with very little of it and the liver needs it to finish making factors II, VII, IX, and X. Bacteria in the gut later help make vitamin K.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that turns liquid blood into a gel at a wound.

tossups.p: Factor V Leiden [“LY-den”], an inherited gene variant that is especially common in people of European ancestry, makes this process harder to switch off. When this process happens inside a blood vessel where it shouldn’t, doctors call it thrombosis.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, which needs platelets and fibrin, that normally stops bleeding.

clues.t: The process that turns liquid blood into a gel-like plug to stop bleeding from a wound
Platelets, tiny cell fragments, stick at a cut and form the first plug
The enzyme thrombin turns the dissolved protein fibrinogen into sticky threads of fibrin
People with hemophilia, an inherited X-linked disorder, have trouble completing it
Needs vitamin K, which the liver uses to make several of the proteins involved
A scab is the dried result of it on the skin
Part of hemostasis: vascular spasm narrows the vessel, platelets form a plug, then fibrin threads strengthen it
Works as a cascade: each activated factor switches on the next, and the factors are numbered with Roman numerals
A classic example of positive feedback, because thrombin speeds up its own production
Needs calcium ions, so blood tubes containing citrate, which grabs calcium, keep samples liquid
Serum is the liquid left afterward: plasma with its fibrinogen used up
Blood thinners such as heparin and warfarin slow it, and aspirin keeps platelets from clumping
Prothrombin (factor II), made in the liver, becomes thrombin, the enzyme that makes fibrin
Hemophilia A means too little factor VIII; hemophilia B means too little factor IX
Henrik Dam named vitamin K for this process’s name in Danish and German; he shared the 1943 Nobel Prize with Edward Doisy
No factor is still called factor VI, factor IV is simply calcium, and factor XIII cross-links fibrin into a sturdy mesh
Hemophilia B is nicknamed Christmas disease after patient Stephen Christmas (1952); a 2009 study found it in Queen Victoria’s descendants
Von Willebrand disease, the most common inherited bleeding disorder, was described in 1926 in Finland’s Åland Islands; its protein glues platelets to collagen
Cattle that ate spoiled sweet clover bled; Karl Paul Link’s lab found dicoumarol and then made warfarin, named for WARF
Jay McLean found heparin in dog liver in 1916; it works by boosting antithrombin
Tissue factor starts the extrinsic pathway; the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways meet at factor X
Plasmin breaks down fibrin, leaving D-dimers; the drug tPA turns plasminogen into plasmin to dissolve blockages
Vampire bat saliva has draculin and leeches make hirudin, both of which block it while the animals feed
An extract of horseshoe crab blood cells turns into a gel around bacterial toxins, a test used on medicines
Aspirin stops platelets from making thromboxane A2, a signal that calls more platelets to a wound
Newborns in many countries get a vitamin K shot, since they are born with very little; the liver needs it for factors II, VII, IX, and X
Factor V Leiden, an inherited variant common in people of European ancestry, makes it harder to switch off; when it happens inside a blood vessel by mistake, that is thrombosis

trap.title: Clotting or clumping?
trap.body: When mismatched blood types are mixed, red cells stick together, but that is agglutination, an antibody reaction, not this process. Players also name a single part of the process, such as platelets, fibrin, or thrombin, or the disorder hemophilia, instead of the process itself.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “this process” that seals wounds or runs as a cascade of numbered factors, say blood clotting or coagulation. Mismatched transfusions and anti-A or anti-B antibodies mean agglutination. Give a part only when the question asks for “these cell fragments,” “this protein,” or “this enzyme.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Blood clotting (accept coagulation; prompt on hemostasis or blood clots; do not accept “agglutination”)

topics.name: Thyroid gland
topics.kicker: Butterfly-shaped gland in the neck · Uses iodine to set metabolism
topics.briefing: Your thyroid gland is shaped like a butterfly and wraps around the front of your windpipe, just below your Adam’s apple. It uses iodine from your food to make hormones called T3 and T4, which set how fast your body burns energy, and it also makes calcitonin, which helps control calcium. Without enough iodine, the gland can swell into a lump called a goiter, which is why table salt is often “iodized.”

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Swiss surgeon Theodor Kocher [“KOKH-er”] won the 1909 Nobel Prize for his work on the surgery and diseases of this gland. Some of his patients who had all of this gland removed developed serious health problems, a clue that it makes essential hormones.
tossups.r: Its hormones control metabolism. For 10 points, name this butterfly-shaped gland in the neck that makes thyroxine.

tossups.p: In 1912, J. F. Gudernatsch [“GOO-der-nahch”] fed tadpoles bits of this gland and found that they turned into tiny frogs much earlier than normal. A hormone from this gland triggers that metamorphosis in amphibians.
tossups.r: In humans, this gland sits in the front of the neck. For 10 points, name this gland whose hormones control metabolism.

tossups.p: Parafollicular [“pair-uh-fuh-LIK-yoo-ler”] cells, or C cells, in this gland make calcitonin, a hormone that lowers the calcium level in the blood. Usually four tiny glands that do the opposite job, raising blood calcium, sit on this gland’s back surface.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this butterfly-shaped gland in the neck that uses iodine to make hormones.

tossups.p: Called Basedow’s [“BAH-zuh-dohz”] disease in much of Europe, Graves’ disease is an autoimmune disorder in which antibodies switch on this gland so that it makes too much hormone. President George H. W. Bush and First Lady Barbara Bush both had it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gland, found in the neck, whose hormones control metabolism.

tossups.p: In 1912, Japanese doctor Hakaru Hashimoto described a condition in which the immune system slowly damages this gland, a common cause of its underactive form. Many people with that condition take levothyroxine [“lee-voh-thy-ROK-seen”], a lab-made copy of this gland’s main hormone.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gland in the neck that makes the hormones T3 and T4.

tossups.p: Starting in 1917, David Marine and O. P. Kimball gave small doses of a supplement to schoolgirls in Akron, Ohio, and showed that it prevented a swelling of this gland that was common around the Great Lakes.
tossups.r: The supplement was iodine, and the swelling is called a goiter. For 10 points, name this gland in the neck.

tossups.p: This gland is built from tiny hollow balls called follicles, each lined with cells and filled with a protein-rich gel called colloid, which stores this gland’s hormones until the body needs them. The cells build those hormones from the amino acid tyrosine.
tossups.r: Those hormones carry four or three iodine atoms each, giving them the names T4 and T3. For 10 points, name this butterfly-shaped gland in the neck.

tossups.p: Edward Kendall, who later shared a Nobel Prize for work on cortisone, isolated this gland’s main hormone in 1914. Charles Harington later worked out that hormone’s structure and made it in a lab.
tossups.r: That hormone, thyroxine, is also called T4. For 10 points, name this gland that wraps around the front of the windpipe.

tossups.p: This gland’s two lobes are joined by a narrow bridge of tissue called the isthmus, and many people also have a small third part called the pyramidal lobe. Its name comes from a Greek word for a shield.
tossups.r: It sits just below the Adam’s apple. For 10 points, name this butterfly-shaped gland in the front of the neck.

tossups.p: The hypothalamus starts a chain of signals by releasing TRH, and high levels of this gland’s hormones later shut that chain down by negative feedback. Doctors often test how well this gland is working by measuring the chain’s middle signal in the blood.
tossups.r: That signal, TSH, comes from the pituitary gland. For 10 points, name this gland that makes thyroxine.

tossups.p: In 1941, Saul Hertz began treating overactive versions of this gland with a radioactive form of an element that this gland collects. After nuclear accidents, people nearby may take potassium iodide pills to keep the radioactive form out of this gland.
tossups.r: That element is iodine, which this gland uses to make its hormones. For 10 points, name this gland in the neck.

tossups.p: Unlike most hormones built from amino acids, this gland’s main hormones enter cells and bind receptors inside the nucleus, where they switch genes on and off. Enzymes in organs such as the liver turn its main product into a more active form by removing one atom.
tossups.r: That atom is iodine, which changes T4 into T3. For 10 points, name this gland whose hormones set the body’s metabolic rate.

tossups.p: Newborn babies in many countries get a heel-prick blood test that checks, among other things, whether this gland is working, since too little of its hormones can slow a baby’s growth and brain development. Early treatment with its hormone helps those babies grow and develop normally.
tossups.r: Those hormones contain iodine. For 10 points, name this gland in the neck that controls metabolism.

tossups.p: The endostyle [“EN-doh-style”], a food-trapping groove in sea squirts and lancelets, is thought to be the ancient version of this gland, and in lampreys the endostyle turns into this gland as the larva grows up.
tossups.r: In humans, this gland makes thyroxine, which helps control metabolism. For 10 points, name this butterfly-shaped gland in the neck.

tossups.p: The axolotl [“AK-suh-lot-ul”], a Mexican salamander that normally keeps its feathery gills for life, can be pushed into changing into an adult form by giving it this gland’s main hormone. Tadpoles whose bodies lack that hormone never turn into frogs.
tossups.r: Its hormones also control human metabolism. For 10 points, name this butterfly-shaped gland in the neck.

clues.t: A butterfly-shaped gland in the front of the neck
Its hormones control metabolism, how fast the body uses energy
Makes the hormones thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3)
Needs iodine to make its hormones, which is why table salt is often “iodized”
A swollen version of it is called a goiter, often caused by too little iodine
The pituitary gland’s TSH tells it to release hormones, and high hormone levels shut TSH off by negative feedback
Its C cells (parafollicular cells) make calcitonin, which lowers blood calcium
Usually four tiny glands on its back surface make a hormone that raises blood calcium
Graves’ disease, the most common cause of an overactive one, is autoimmune: antibodies switch it on
Hashimoto’s disease (described in 1912) is an autoimmune cause of an underactive one, often treated with levothyroxine
Its hormones are built from the amino acid tyrosine plus iodine atoms: four in T4, three in T3
Its main hormone triggers metamorphosis in tadpoles and other amphibians
Its name comes from a Greek word for a shield
It sits just below the Adam’s apple and wraps around the front of the windpipe
Swiss surgeon Theodor Kocher won the 1909 Nobel Prize for his work on its surgery and diseases
Edward Kendall isolated its main hormone, thyroxine, in 1914; Charles Harington later worked out its structure
In 1912, J. F. Gudernatsch fed tadpoles tissue from it, and they became frogs early
Its hormone can push an axolotl, a salamander that keeps its gills, into an adult form; tadpoles lacking that hormone never become frogs
Built of hollow follicles filled with colloid, a gel made mostly of the protein thyroglobulin
Its two lobes are joined by a bridge called the isthmus; many people also have a small pyramidal lobe
TRH from the hypothalamus starts its control chain, and doctors check how well it works by measuring TSH in the blood
Saul Hertz began treating overactive ones with radioactive iodine in 1941; potassium iodide pills after nuclear accidents keep radioactive iodine out of it
David Marine and O. P. Kimball’s study of Akron, Ohio, schoolgirls (from 1917) showed that iodine prevents goiters, once common around the Great Lakes
Graves’ disease is called Basedow’s disease in much of Europe; George H. W. Bush and Barbara Bush both had it
Its hormones bind receptors inside the nucleus; organs such as the liver turn T4 into the more active T3 by removing one iodine atom
Newborns get a heel-prick test that checks whether it works, since too little of its hormone can slow growth and brain development
The endostyle, a food-trapping groove in sea squirts, lancelets, and larval lampreys, is thought to be its ancient version

trap.title: Thyroid, parathyroid, or thymus?
trap.body: Three glands sound alike. The parathyroid glands, usually four tiny glands on the back of this one, raise blood calcium, while this gland’s calcitonin lowers it. The thymus, in the chest behind the breastbone, trains T cells. Players also answer a hormone (thyroxine or TSH) or the swelling (goiter) instead of the gland.
trap.fix: A butterfly shape, iodine, thyroxine, T3 and T4, calcitonin, goiters, or metabolism mean the thyroid. Parathyroid hormone or “four tiny glands” mean the parathyroids, and T cells maturing means the thymus. If the question asks for “this gland,” don’t answer a hormone.
trap.line: Real answer line: Thyroid gland (do not accept “parathyroid glands” or “thymus”)

topics.name: Bacterial conjugation
topics.kicker: How bacteria share plasmids · DNA passed through a pilus
topics.briefing: Bacteria can swap genes without making new cells. In bacterial conjugation, a donor cell reaches out with a thin tube called a pilus, pulls a neighbor close, and passes it a copy of a plasmid, a small ring of DNA. It is a big reason genes for surviving antibiotics can spread quickly from one bacterium to another, sometimes even between different species.
topics.answerHtml: Conjugation (accept bacterial conjugation; prompt on horizontal gene transfer or lateral gene transfer; do not accept “transformation” or “transduction”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1946, Joshua Lederberg and Edward Tatum mixed two strains of E. coli that each could not make certain nutrients, and found new cells that could make all of them. To rule out simple mutation, each strain lacked several abilities at once. That result revealed this process.
tossups.r: In this process, a donor bacterium passes a plasmid through a tube called a pilus. For 10 points, name this way that bacteria share genes.

tossups.p: In 1950, Bernard Davis put two bacterial strains in the two arms of a U-shaped tube, separated by a filter that let liquid but not cells pass through, and found that this process could not happen without direct contact.
tossups.r: That showed it differs from transformation, in which bacteria pick up loose DNA. For 10 points, name this process in which bacteria pass plasmids through a pilus.

tossups.p: Élie Wollman and François Jacob mapped bacterial genes by stopping this process at set times with a kitchen blender, which is why the E. coli gene map is measured in minutes. Genes closest to the starting point entered the recipient first.
tossups.r: In this process, a donor bacterium passes DNA to a neighbor through a pilus. For 10 points, name this form of horizontal gene transfer.

tossups.p: In Hfr strains, short for “high frequency of recombination,” the F plasmid has joined the main chromosome, so this process can carry chromosome genes into another cell in a fixed order. Transferring a whole chromosome this way takes about 100 minutes, so the cells usually separate first.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process in which one bacterium passes DNA to another through a tube called a pilus.

tossups.p: Esther Lederberg helped discover the F factor, a plasmid that lets the cells carrying it start this process. When an F-positive cell completes this process with an F-negative cell, the recipient becomes F-positive, too.
tossups.r: Afterward, both cells have a copy of the plasmid. For 10 points, name this process in which bacteria pass copies of plasmids through a pilus.

tossups.p: To begin this process, an enzyme cuts just one strand of a plasmid’s DNA ring, and that single strand slides into the recipient cell. The donor rebuilds its own copy by rolling-circle replication, while the recipient builds a matching second strand.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process in which a bacterium passes a plasmid to a neighbor through a pilus.

tossups.p: Agrobacterium tumefaciens [“ag-roh-bak-TEER-ee-um too-muh-FAY-shee-enz”] uses machinery related to this process to move DNA from its Ti plasmid into plant cells, causing lumpy growths called crown galls. Scientists borrow that system to put new genes into crops.
tossups.r: In ordinary bacteria, this process sends a copy of a plasmid through a tube called a pilus. For 10 points, name this way that bacteria share genes.

tossups.p: The scientist who coined the word “plasmid” in 1952 shared the 1958 Nobel Prize partly for discovering this process, and he was only 33 years old when he won. He shared that prize with Edward Tatum and George Beadle.
tossups.r: That scientist was Joshua Lederberg. For 10 points, name this process in which a bacterium passes DNA to another through a pilus.

tossups.p: Plasmids called R factors, which can carry genes for resistance to several antibiotics at once, often spread between gut bacteria by this process, even between different species. They were discovered in Japan after dysentery bacteria that resisted several drugs at once appeared there in the 1950s.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process in which a donor bacterium sends a copy of a plasmid through a tube called a pilus.

tossups.p: Many bacteria carry out this process using a type IV secretion system, a protein machine that spans the cell envelope and pushes DNA into a partner cell. Genes on the plasmid itself build that machine, including the pilus.
tossups.r: It is one way that genes for antibiotic resistance spread. For 10 points, name this process of plasmid transfer between bacteria that are touching.

tossups.p: Paramecia swap small nuclei called micronuclei in a process that shares this process’s name, and the green alga Spirogyra [“spy-roh-JY-ruh”] joins side-by-side filaments with tubes in another process with the same name.
tossups.r: In bacteria, this process sends a copy of a plasmid through a pilus. For 10 points, name this process, a form of horizontal gene transfer.

tossups.p: When an F plasmid pops out of the chromosome and takes a few chromosome genes with it, it becomes an F-prime plasmid, which can then carry those genes into new cells during this process.
tossups.r: Unlike binary fission, this process makes no new cells. For 10 points, name this process in which bacteria share plasmids through a pilus.

tossups.p: The thin appendage that starts this process can latch onto a partner cell and then shrink back, reeling the two cells together. Only cells carrying certain plasmids can build that appendage.
tossups.r: That appendage is called a pilus. For 10 points, name this process in which a donor bacterium passes DNA to a recipient.

tossups.p: This process needs no virus, unlike transduction, which Norton Zinder and Joshua Lederberg discovered in 1952, and no loose DNA, unlike transformation, which Frederick Griffith first saw in 1928.
tossups.r: Instead, two living cells touch, and a plasmid passes through a pilus. For 10 points, name this way that bacteria share genes.

tossups.p: Bacteria can even use this process to pass plasmids into yeast cells, which belong to a different kingdom of life. Genes moved this way are one example of horizontal gene transfer, which spreads genes without parents passing them to offspring.
tossups.r: Usually, this process moves a plasmid from one bacterium to another through a pilus. For 10 points, name this process.

clues.t: A donor bacterium passes DNA to a recipient through a thin tube called a pilus
Usually moves a copy of a plasmid, a small ring of DNA separate from the main chromosome
A form of horizontal gene transfer: genes pass between living cells, not from parent to offspring
Needs direct contact between two living cells
Spreads genes for antibiotic resistance from one bacterium to another
Discovered by Joshua Lederberg and Edward Tatum in 1946, using E. coli strains that each couldn’t make certain nutrients
The F plasmid lets a cell start it: F-positive cells are donors and F-negative cells are recipients
Afterward, the recipient has its own copy of the F plasmid and can become a donor too
It is not reproduction, since no new cells are made; bacteria reproduce by binary fission
Unlike transformation (loose DNA; Griffith, 1928) or transduction (carried by phages; Zinder and Lederberg, 1952), it needs cell contact
Only one strand of the plasmid crosses over, and each cell then rebuilds a double-stranded copy
R factors are plasmids carrying resistance to several antibiotics; they were found in Japan after multidrug-resistant dysentery bacteria appeared in the 1950s
Bernard Davis’s U-tube experiment (1950) showed it needs contact: a filter between two strains stopped it
Élie Wollman and François Jacob stopped it at set times in a kitchen blender to map genes, so the E. coli gene map is measured in minutes
In Hfr (“high frequency of recombination”) strains, the F plasmid has joined the chromosome; passing a whole chromosome takes about 100 minutes
Esther Lederberg helped discover the F plasmid, also called the F factor
Joshua Lederberg coined the word “plasmid” (1952) and shared the 1958 Nobel Prize, at age 33, with Tatum and George Beadle
An enzyme nicks one strand of the plasmid to start it, and the donor replaces the strand it sends by rolling-circle replication
Its machinery is a type IV secretion system, built by genes on the plasmid itself
Agrobacterium tumefaciens uses related machinery to move DNA from its Ti plasmid into plants, causing crown galls
An F plasmid that leaves the chromosome carrying extra genes is an F-prime plasmid
Paramecia (which swap micronuclei) and the alga Spirogyra (which joins filaments with tubes) carry out processes with the same name
Bacteria can even pass plasmids to yeast cells this way, crossing into another kingdom
The pilus latches onto a partner cell and then shrinks back, reeling the two cells together

trap.title: Three ways to swap genes
trap.body: Bacteria share genes in three main ways, and tossups often name one to rule it out. In transformation, a cell picks up loose DNA from its surroundings (Griffith’s 1928 experiment); in transduction, a virus called a phage carries DNA from cell to cell. Conjugation is the only one that needs two living cells to touch, usually through a pilus.
trap.fix: A pilus, the F plasmid, F-positive and F-negative cells, Hfr strains, or a U-tube experiment mean conjugation. Loose DNA or “rough” and “smooth” strains mean transformation, and phages mean transduction. Don’t answer “binary fission”: that is how bacteria reproduce, not how they share genes.
trap.line: Real answer line: Conjugation (accept bacterial conjugation; prompt on horizontal gene transfer or lateral gene transfer; do not accept “transformation” or “transduction”)

topics.name: Testosterone
topics.kicker: Steroid hormone made mainly in the testes · Builds muscle and bone
topics.dates: Isolated and first made in a lab in 1935
topics.briefing: Testosterone is a steroid hormone made mainly in the testes, with smaller amounts made by the ovaries and adrenal glands. During puberty it fuels a growth spurt, builds muscle and bone, and lengthens the vocal cords so the voice deepens. In 1935, scientists in Amsterdam isolated it, and teams led by Adolf Butenandt and Leopold Ružička made it in the lab; the two chemists shared the 1939 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
topics.answerHtml: Testosterone (prompt on androgen or steroid hormone; do not accept “estrogen,” “estradiol,” or “dihydrotestosterone”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Adolf Butenandt and Leopold Ružička [“ROO-zhich-kah”] each found a way to make this hormone in the lab in 1935, and they shared the 1939 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The Nazi government forced Butenandt to turn the prize down, but he accepted it after World War II.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this hormone, made mainly in the testes, that helps build muscle and bone.

tossups.p: In 1935, Ernst Laqueur’s team in Amsterdam isolated crystals of this hormone from bull tissue and gave it its name, which blends a word for the organ that makes most of it with “sterol” and the chemical ending “-one.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this hormone that causes a growth spurt and a deeper voice during puberty.

tossups.p: An enzyme called aromatase converts this hormone into estradiol, a form of estrogen, by turning one of its carbon rings into a benzene-like ring. Fat tissue and the brain both contain that enzyme.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this steroid hormone, made mainly in the testes, that builds muscle and bone.

tossups.p: Leydig [“LY-dig”] cells, named for German scientist Franz Leydig, make most of this hormone after receiving a signal called luteinizing [“LOO-tee-uh-nye-zing”] hormone, or LH, from the pituitary gland. Leydig first described those cells in 1850.
tossups.r: It is made mainly in the testes. For 10 points, name this hormone that builds muscle and bone mass during puberty.

tossups.p: This hormone has the chemical formula C19H28O2, and like all steroids it has four fused rings of carbon atoms. Cells build it from cholesterol, passing through pregnenolone [“preg-NEE-nuh-lohn”] along the way.
tossups.r: It also deepens the voice during puberty. For 10 points, name this hormone, made mainly in the testes, that increases muscle and bone growth.

tossups.p: In 1849, Arnold Berthold showed that a rooster’s comb and crowing depended on a substance that certain glands sent through the blood, an early experiment in endocrinology. That substance was later identified as this hormone.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this hormone, made mainly in the testes, that helps build muscle and bone.

tossups.p: In deer, rising levels of this hormone in late summer make antlers harden and shed their velvet, and falling levels in winter make the antlers drop off. In lions, the hormone helps males grow their manes.
tossups.r: In humans, it is made mainly in the testes and builds muscle and bone. For 10 points, name this hormone.

tossups.p: Lab-made relatives of this hormone, called anabolic steroids, are banned in sports by the World Anti-Doping Agency. The word “anabolic” refers to building up the body’s tissues, such as muscle.
tossups.r: It is the main androgen. For 10 points, name this hormone, made mainly in the testes, that drives muscle and bone growth during puberty.

tossups.p: Like other steroid hormones, this hormone travels through the blood mostly attached to carrier proteins such as albumin. It enlarges the larynx, thickens the vocal folds, and makes the skin’s sebaceous [“sih-BAY-shus”] glands release more oil.
tossups.r: Those changes deepen the voice and can cause acne during puberty. For 10 points, name this hormone made mainly in the testes.

tossups.p: This hormone raises the number of red blood cells, partly by boosting the kidneys’ release of erythropoietin [“ih-RITH-roh-POY-ih-tin”]. Partly because of that effect, men usually have more red blood cells than women. It also increases bone density.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this hormone that builds muscle and is made mainly in the testes.

tossups.p: Being a steroid, this hormone passes through cell membranes and binds a protein called the androgen receptor inside cells, which then switches on certain genes in the nucleus. DHT, a stronger hormone made from this one, binds that receptor even more tightly.
tossups.r: It helps build muscle and bone. For 10 points, name this hormone made mainly in the testes.

tossups.p: The outer layer of the adrenal glands makes DHEA, which the body can turn into this hormone, and the ovaries also make small amounts of it. Its level in the blood is usually highest in the morning.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this androgen, made mainly in the testes, that helps build muscle and bone.

tossups.p: Estradiol made from this hormone eventually signals the growth plates of long bones to close, which is why people eventually stop growing taller. Those plates are disks of cartilage near the ends of the bones.
tossups.r: Before that, this hormone fuels the teenage growth spurt. For 10 points, name this hormone made mainly in the testes.

tossups.p: The enzyme 5-alpha reductase turns this hormone into DHT, a stronger androgen that is linked to hair loss on the top of the scalp. That enzyme is especially active in the skin and hair follicles.
tossups.r: This hormone and DHT both help facial hair grow during puberty. For 10 points, name this hormone made mainly in the testes.

tossups.p: The hypothalamus releases GnRH, which tells the pituitary to release LH, which in turn tells the body to make more of this hormone. High levels of this hormone then slow that chain down by negative feedback.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this hormone, made mainly in the testes, that builds muscle and bone.

clues.t: A hormone made mainly in the testes
Builds muscle and bone, especially during puberty
The main androgen, a type of steroid hormone
During puberty it drives a growth spurt, a deeper voice, and facial hair
Made from cholesterol, like other steroid hormones, and has four fused carbon rings
Leydig cells in the testes make most of it
Luteinizing hormone (LH) from the pituitary gland tells Leydig cells to make it
Everyone makes some: the ovaries and adrenal glands make smaller amounts, and the adrenals’ DHEA can be turned into it
The enzyme aromatase turns it into estradiol, a form of estrogen
The enzyme 5-alpha reductase turns it into DHT, a stronger androgen
It raises red blood cell production and bone density
Lab-made relatives called anabolic steroids are banned in sports
It enlarges the larynx, deepening the voice, and makes skin oil glands more active, one cause of teenage acne
Adolf Butenandt and Leopold Ružička each made it in the lab in 1935 and shared the 1939 Chemistry Nobel; the Nazi government made Butenandt wait until after World War II to accept
Ernst Laqueur’s team in Amsterdam isolated and named it in 1935; the name blends the organ’s name with “sterol” and the ending “-one”
Its formula is C19H28O2, and cells make it from cholesterol by way of pregnenolone
Arnold Berthold’s 1849 rooster experiments showed that a substance carried in the blood made combs grow, an early experiment in endocrinology
In deer, rising levels make antlers harden and shed velvet, and falling levels make antlers drop; it also helps male lions grow manes
It boosts the kidneys’ release of erythropoietin, one reason men usually have more red blood cells than women
It passes through cell membranes and binds the androgen receptor inside cells; DHT binds that receptor even more tightly
It travels in the blood mostly attached to carrier proteins such as albumin
Its level in the blood is usually highest in the morning
Estradiol made from it eventually closes the growth plates of long bones, so growth in height stops
DHT made from it is linked to hair loss on the top of the scalp
GnRH from the hypothalamus starts its control chain, and high levels of it shut the chain down by negative feedback

trap.title: Which steroid hormone?
trap.body: Tossups on this hormone mention its close chemical relatives: estradiol, which aromatase makes from it; DHT, a stronger androgen made from it; DHEA from the adrenal glands; and cholesterol, the starting material for every steroid hormone. Buzzing with a relative loses the tossup, and so does naming the organ instead of the hormone.
trap.fix: Leydig cells, LH, Butenandt and Ružička, C19H28O2, or “the main androgen” mean testosterone. If a clue says a hormone is made from this one (estradiol by aromatase, DHT by 5-alpha reductase), the answer is still the starting hormone. Saying just “androgen” or “steroid” earns a prompt, so be ready to name it.
trap.line: Real answer line: Testosterone (prompt on androgen or steroid hormone; do not accept “estrogen,” “estradiol,” or “dihydrotestosterone”)

topics.name: Diabetes
topics.kicker: A disease of high blood sugar · Linked to the hormone insulin
topics.briefing: Diabetes is a disease in which the level of sugar in the blood stays too high, because the pancreas makes too little insulin or the body’s cells don’t respond to it well. In type 1, the immune system destroys the cells that make insulin; in type 2, the most common form, cells resist insulin’s signal. People with diabetes check their blood sugar and may take insulin by pen, shot, or pump, a treatment first used in 1922.
topics.answerHtml: Diabetes mellitus (accept type 1 or type 2 diabetes; prompt on hyperglycemia or high blood sugar; do not accept “diabetes insipidus”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In the 1670s, English doctor Thomas Willis noted that the urine of people with this disease was sweet, and a Latin word meaning “honey-sweet” became part of the disease’s full name. The Greek-based first word of that name means “to pass through,” because people with it urinate often.
tossups.r: People with this disease check their blood sugar and may take insulin. For 10 points, name this disease in which blood sugar runs too high.

tossups.p: Ancient Indian doctors called this disease madhumeha [“MUH-dhoo-MAY-hah”], or “honey urine,” after noticing that ants were drawn to the urine of people who had it. The Greek doctor Aretaeus [“air-uh-TEE-us”] of Cappadocia also wrote a famous early description of it.
tossups.r: Many people with it use insulin pens or pumps. For 10 points, name this disease marked by high blood sugar.

tossups.p: In 1889, Oskar Minkowski and Joseph von Mering found that dogs whose pancreas had been removed developed this disease. Twenty years earlier, Paul Langerhans had described small clusters of cells in that organ, later named for him.
tossups.r: In type 1 of this disease, the immune system destroys the pancreas’s insulin-making beta cells. For 10 points, name this disease.

tossups.p: Elizabeth Hughes, daughter of U.S. Secretary of State Charles Evans Hughes, was one of the earliest patients treated with a new hormone for this disease in 1922. That January, a teenage boy named Leonard Thompson had become the first person given that hormone, at Toronto General Hospital.
tossups.r: That hormone was insulin, which people with type 1 of this disease need every day. For 10 points, name this disease marked by high blood sugar.

tossups.p: Metformin, a common medicine for one form of this disease, was developed from galegine [“GAL-uh-jeen”], a chemical in goat’s rue, a flowering plant also called French lilac. Doctors in Europe began prescribing it in the late 1950s.
tossups.r: In that form, called type 2, the body’s cells respond poorly to insulin. For 10 points, name this disease marked by high blood sugar.

tossups.p: If people with this disease have too little of a certain hormone, their bodies burn fat and make acids called ketones, which can build up dangerously and give the breath a fruity smell. That emergency is called ketoacidosis [“kee-toh-ass-ih-DOH-sis”].
tossups.r: It happens most often in type 1 of this disease, in which the body makes almost no insulin. For 10 points, name this disease marked by high blood sugar.

tossups.p: Frederick Banting got the idea for his research on this disease in October 1920, after reading an article about what happens when the pancreas’s ducts get blocked. He later carried out that research with Charles Best in J. J. R. Macleod’s lab.
tossups.r: Their work produced insulin, which people with type 1 of this disease need. For 10 points, name this disease.

tossups.p: The United Nations officially recognized this disease’s worldwide awareness day in 2006; it falls on November 14, the birthday of a Canadian scientist. The day’s symbol is a blue circle.
tossups.r: That scientist, Frederick Banting, helped discover insulin. For 10 points, name this disease in which blood sugar runs too high.

tossups.p: In London, Ontario, a “Flame of Hope” burns near the house where Frederick Banting lived when he got his big idea, and it is meant to be put out only when a cure for this disease is found.
tossups.r: People with this disease may use insulin pumps. For 10 points, name this disease marked by high blood sugar.

tossups.p: Doctors call three classic warning signs of this disease the “three P’s”: polyuria [“pah-lee-YOOR-ee-uh”], or frequent urination; polydipsia [“pah-lee-DIP-see-uh”], or extreme thirst; and polyphagia [“pah-lee-FAY-jee-uh”], or extreme hunger. Many people also feel very tired or notice blurry vision.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease in which the body makes too little insulin or uses it poorly.

tossups.p: In the most common form of this disease, muscle and fat cells fail to move enough GLUT4 transporter proteins to their surfaces when a certain hormone signals them. That form makes up about 90 to 95 percent of all cases.
tossups.r: That form, type 2, is marked by insulin resistance. For 10 points, name this disease marked by high blood sugar.

tossups.p: Sonia Sotomayor, who joined the U.S. Supreme Court in 2009, learned she had this disease at age seven. Her picture book _Just Ask!_ features a girl named Sonia who lives with it.
tossups.r: She has type 1, in which the body makes almost no insulin. For 10 points, name this disease marked by high blood sugar.

tossups.p: Doctors track this disease with the A1C test, which measures glycated [“GLY-kay-ted”] hemoglobin inside red blood cells and reflects average levels over the past two to three months. Glycated means that sugar molecules have stuck to the protein.
tossups.r: Some people with this disease link a glucose sensor to an insulin pump to make an “artificial pancreas.” For 10 points, name this disease.

tossups.p: Eye doctors look for damage that this disease can cause to the tiny blood vessels of the retina, and over many years it can also harm the kidneys and the nerves in the feet.
tossups.r: That damage happens when blood sugar stays too high for a long time. For 10 points, name this disease treated with insulin.

tossups.p: A rare condition linked to the hormone ADH, also called vasopressin, shares the first word of this disease’s name, but its Latin second word means “tasteless,” because the large amounts of urine it causes contain no sugar.
tossups.r: This disease, by contrast, is marked by high blood sugar. For 10 points, name this disease whose type 1 and type 2 forms involve insulin.

clues.t: A disease in which blood sugar (glucose) stays too high
Caused by too little insulin or by cells that respond poorly to it; many people with it take insulin
Two main types: type 1 (the immune system destroys insulin-making cells) and type 2 (cells respond poorly to insulin)
The pancreas’s beta cells make the insulin that keeps blood sugar in check
People with it check their blood sugar with finger-prick meters or sensors and may use insulin pens or pumps
Type 1 is autoimmune and often starts in childhood; it was once called “juvenile”
Type 2 makes up about 90 to 95 percent of cases and often runs in families

The A1C test measures sugar stuck to hemoglobin over the past two to three months
Frederick Banting and Charles Best discovered insulin in Toronto in 1921, giving people with it a treatment
Its Greek name means “to pass through”; its full name adds a Latin word meaning “honey-sweet”

An “artificial pancreas” links a glucose sensor to an insulin pump

The Greek doctor Aretaeus of Cappadocia wrote a famous early description of it

Leonard Thompson, a teenage boy, was the first person treated with insulin (Toronto General Hospital, January 1922); Elizabeth Hughes was another early patient
Metformin, a common type 2 medicine, was developed from galegine, a chemical in goat’s rue (French lilac)
With too little insulin, the body makes ketones that can build up dangerously (ketoacidosis), sometimes with fruity-smelling breath
Banting got his idea in October 1920 after reading about blocked pancreatic ducts; he worked in J. J. R. Macleod’s lab

trap.title: Mellitus or insipidus?
trap.body: Two different conditions share the word “diabetes,” from the Greek for “to pass through,” because both make people urinate a lot. Diabetes mellitus (“honey-sweet”) is about blood sugar and insulin. Diabetes insipidus (“tasteless”) is a rare water-balance problem involving the hormone ADH, and a question about the sugar disease won’t accept it. Others buzz with “insulin” or “pancreas,” the hormone or the organ, instead of the disease.
trap.fix: Insulin, beta cells, glucose, the A1C test, or Banting and Best mean diabetes mellitus (plain “diabetes” is fine). ADH, vasopressin, or urine with no sugar mean diabetes insipidus. If the question asks for “this hormone” or “this organ,” answer insulin or pancreas instead.
trap.line: Real answer line: Diabetes mellitus (accept type 1 or type 2 diabetes; prompt on hyperglycemia or high blood sugar; do not accept “diabetes insipidus”)
